# DataWeave performance and large payloads

Reference for [the DataWeave rules](../../../instructions/dataweave.instructions.md). Read it before optimizing a script, reading large inputs, or changing lookups or streaming. Items marked (documented) are stated in MuleSoft documentation; items marked (CLI) were observed with the DataWeave CLI (runtime 2.12.2, language levels 2.4–2.9) and should be confirmed on the project's runtime when they decide the outcome.

No construct is universally faster. Ask for or state the expected payload size, then change performance only with a reason you can measure on the target runtime. CLI timings come from a native binary, not Mule's JVM; use them for relative scale only.

- Compute anything reused (a lookup table, a grouped collection, a parsed value) once, in a variable outside the `map`. DataWeave did not cache it for you: `groupBy` inside the `map` lambda, or in a `do` variable inside it, ran once per record (16,000 records: about 23 s, against 0.04 s when built once). Calling a function twice with the same arguments cost twice as much, and an unused `do` variable was still computed; a variable used twice was computed once (CLI).
- For repeated equality lookups, consider building `groupBy` once or using `dw::core::Arrays` `join`/`leftJoin` only when matching, duplicate, null and ordering semantics remain equivalent. Join criteria are strings; replacing a strict numeric/string comparison can create new matches. See [join](https://docs.mulesoft.com/dataweave/2.9/dw-arrays-functions-join). Measure before replacing a nested filter or an object lookup table. With 16,000 records and 4,000 keys, the nested filter took about 8 s, `groupBy` 0.06 s and `join` 0.08 s; 32,000 lookups into a 32,000-key object built with `{(... map ...)}` took about 3.5 s, against 0.2 s through `groupBy` (CLI).
- Use `maxBy` or `minBy` for the largest or smallest item, not `orderBy(...)[0]`: at 800,000 items, 1 s against 12.6 s (CLI). Sort only when the contract needs order. `filter(...)[0]`, `firstWith` and `some` stopped at the first match (CLI), so they need no rewrite.
- Map only the fields the output needs, and avoid needless format conversions. Selecting 3 of 23 fields halved the time and cut output about 6 times; rebuilding every field with `mapObject` took about 1.7 times as long as passing records through; a `read(write(...))` round trip took about 5 times as long through JSON and 8 times through XML as mapping directly (CLI).
- For large responses, `indent=false` cut JSON output by about a third and XML writing time by about 30% (CLI). See [app design for performance](https://docs.mulesoft.com/mule-runtime/4.9/tuning-app-design).
- Runtime type checks on complex object parameters cost time: a function with a typed object parameter, called 200,000 times, took about 3 times as long as an untyped one, and `@DesignOnlyType()` on the parameter removed the difference (CLI). Keep the types; use `@DesignOnlyType()` on hot paths when the input is already validated. See [annotations](https://docs.mulesoft.com/dataweave/2.9/dw-core-annotations).
- Choose the reading strategy deliberately. Large inputs are indexed on disk automatically. Streaming needs the `streaming=true` reader property (XML also needs `collectionPath`, the path to the element that contains the repeating items) and a script that reads the input once, sequentially; sorting, grouping or a second read defeats that access pattern. For XML it mattered: a 53 MB file took 4.6 s and 1.8 GB of memory without streaming, against 1.5 s and 190 MB with it. For JSON (28 and 115 MB) and CSV (36 MB) single-pass filters it gave no gain. A streamed JSON input read twice without `@StreamCapable()` did not fail but used 1.15 GB, against 175 MB without streaming (CLI). For static validation, put the experimental `@StreamCapable()` annotation on an explicit input directive, for example followed by `input payload application/json`; it rejects repeated references and other unsupported access patterns. Verify memory behavior on the target runtime. See [streaming](https://docs.mulesoft.com/dataweave/2.9/dataweave-streaming) and [indexed readers](https://docs.mulesoft.com/dataweave/2.9/dataweave-indexed-readers).
- Prefer `map`, `flatMap`, `filter`, `groupBy` and `distinctBy` for readability. A `reduce` that appends with `++` was not dramatically slower (32,000 items: about 26 ms versus 15 ms for `map`), building a string with `reduce` was faster than `joinBy`, and regular expressions cost about the same as `startsWith` or a plain-string `replace` (CLI). Combining a `filter`, `map` and `distinctBy` chain into one `reduce` made it slower (400,000 records: 2.9 s against 1.6 s), and `countBy` cost the same as `sizeOf(filter(...))` (CLI). Do not rewrite working code for speed without a measurement.
- For large `multipart/form-data` parts, use the `^raw` selector when the content does not need parsing.
